extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of geometry/classical mathematics; readers of Archimedes
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of Archimedes' propositions, definitions, and constructive criteria concerning centres of gravity of plane figures (triangles, trapezia, parabolic segments) and his numerical/assumptive framework in The Sand-Reckoner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 14 — centre of gravity of triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of gravity of any triangle is at the intersection of the lines drawn from any two angles to the middle points of the opposite sides respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the lines from two vertices to the midpoints of the opposite sides; their intersection is the centroid. (This follows immediately from the preceding proposition.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 15 — centre of gravity of a trapezium (parallel sides AD, BC)
rubrics_metrics.description: If AD, BC be the two parallel sides of a trapezium ABCD, AD being the smaller, and if AD, BC be bisected at K, H, F respectively, then the centre of gravity of the trapezium was at a point G on EF such that GE:GF = (2 BC + AD) : (2 AD + BC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction and proof: produce BA, CD to meet at O; use centres of gravity of triangles OAD and OBC (on OL and OF) and Prop. 8 and Prop. 13; join BD, divide into three equal parts, draw parallels, identify centres of gravity of component triangles (points H, K) and find intersection OF, HK = G. The ratio VG:GW and area ratios yield GE:GF = (2BC+AD):(2AD+BC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition (Book II, Prop. 1) — centre of gravity of two parabolic segments
rubrics_metrics.description: If P, P' be two parabolic segments and D, E their centres of gravity respectively, the centre of gravity of the two segments taken together will be at a point C on DE determined by the relation given (via substitution by equal rectangles/parallelograms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes substitutes rectangles equal in area to the parabolic segments (using results from the Quadrature of the Parabola) so that the centres coincide with constructed points; by placing equal-area rectangles and parallelograms appropriately one obtains DK = CE and KC = CL and hence C as required. (Note: author remarks this is a special case of Props. 6,7 of Book I.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — 'inscribed in the recognised manner' in a parabolic segment
rubrics_metrics.description: A figure is 'inscribed in the recognised manner' in a parabolic segment when a triangle having the same base and equal height is inscribed, then triangles are recursively inscribed in the remaining segments with same bases and equal heights, continuing similarly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes lists immediate consequences to be proved: (1) lines joining the two angles nearest the vertex and corresponding pairs are parallel to the base; (2) those lines are bisected by the diameter of the segment; (3) they cut the diameter in the proportions of the successive odd numbers (the number one referring to the length adjacent to the vertex). These properties are used in later propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 2 — centroid of an inscribed figure lies on diameter
rubrics_metrics.description: If a figure be 'inscribed in the recognised manner' in a parabolic segment, the centre of gravity of the figure so inscribed will lie on the diameter of the segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompose the inscribed figure into trapezia and a triangle whose centres lie on parallel lines meeting the diameter; hence the combined centre lies on the diameter (uses the decomposition into symmetric pieces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 3 — proportional division of diameters by centres of similar inscribed figures
rubrics_metrics.description: If BAB', bab' be two similar parabolic segments whose diameters are AO, ao respectively, and if a figure be inscribed in each segment 'in the recognised manner' with equal numbers of sides, the centres of gravity of the inscribed figures will divide AO, ao in the same ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Join corresponding vertices, use lemma about divisions by successive odd numbers and proportions of corresponding trapezia/triangles; corresponding centres of gravity of component pieces divide associated diameters in the same proportion, hence the full figures' centres divide AO, ao in same ratio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 4 — centroid of any parabolic segment lies on its diameter
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of gravity of any parabolic segment cut off by a straight line lies on the diameter of the segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: assume centre not on diameter, construct an inscribed figure in the recognised manner whose centroid lies on the diameter (Prop. 2), compare areas so that the centroid of the leftover small segments would have to lie on a line which makes that impossible (segments lie on one side). Uses Quadrature of the Parabola to bound areas and the impossibility argument (Postulate 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 5 — centroid of segment nearer vertex than centroid of any inscribed figure
rubrics_metrics.description: If in a parabolic segment a figure be inscribed 'in the recognised manner', the centre of gravity of the segment is nearer to the vertex of the segment than the centre of gravity of the inscribed figure is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First show for the basic inscribed triangle: centroid of triangle is at AF with AF:FO relation; then compare with centres of the symmetric leftover segments; extend inductively to any inscribed figure by decomposing into triangles and segments and comparing midpoints and proportional distances (uses Props.1–4 and area ratios).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 6 — arbitrarily close inscribed approximations to centroid
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a parabolic segment, it is possible to inscribe in it 'in the recognised manner' a figure such that the distance between the centres of gravity of the segment and of the inscribed figure is less than any assigned length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an inscribed figure so that the sum of remaining small segments is less than a chosen area S derived from the assigned length D and known area ratios; show by contradiction that otherwise the small remaining segments' centroid would lie on the wrong side of a line, impossible because all those segments are on one side. Uses Prop. 5 and the fact that inscribed figures can make remainders arbitrarily small (Quadrature of the Parabola, Prop.20).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 7 — similarity implies same division ratio of diameters
rubrics_metrics.description: If there be two similar parabolic segments, their centres of gravity divide their diameters in the same ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume contrary, choose H on AO with AH:HO = ag:go, inscribe figures with sufficiently small differences (Prop.6), derive contradiction by applying Prop.3 to inscribed figures and using Prop.5 inequalities, hence centres must divide AO, ao in same ratio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 8 — centroid divides diameter 3:1 (AG = 3·GO)
rubrics_metrics.description: If AO be the diameter of a parabolic segment, and G its centre of gravity, then AG = 3·GO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the basic inscribed triangle ABB' and diameters/centres of the two subsegments AQB and AQ'B'. Use relations from Lemmas (including AO = 4·QD) and properties of parallel lines and equal segments to derive area ratios and apply I.6,7 to get KG = 3·GF and other relations; after algebraic combination deduce AG = 3·GO. (This is the classical 3:1 centroid result for a parabolic segment measured along the axis.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 9 (Lemma) — algebraic proportion lemma for continued proportion lines
rubrics_metrics.description: If a, b, c, d be four lines in continued proportion and in descending order, and certain proportional relations hold (given in the text), then it is required to prove that e + y = 2a (a specific linear relation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes provides an algebraic-geometric derivation transforming geometric equalities to algebraic relations, manipulating ratios stepwise (Eutocius-style commentary notes interpolation). The lemma is used in Prop.10 to relate summed lengths to twice a given diameter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 10 — centroid for portion of parabola between two parallel chords
rubrics_metrics.description: For the portion of a parabola intercepted between two parallel chords PP', BB' (bisected by ANO at N,O) and where NO is divided into five equal parts with LM the middle one, if G is point on LM such that LG:GM = BO'·(2PN + BO) : PN'·(2BO + PN), then G is the centre of gravity of the area PP'B'B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes constructs auxiliary similar segments on a scaled line ao,aq,an,ap in continued proportion, measures GF on GA so that OP:G P equals OP, and then uses a chain of proportional equalities connecting area ratios, ordinates, and the previously proven Prop.9 lemma to show GF + OG = OF = 2·AO, which (with Prop.8) gives F as centroid of a related segment and hence G is centroid of the target area by area-composition (I.6,7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption set (The Sand-Reckoner) — astronomical/measurement assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of explicit assumptions used to bound astronomical magnitudes and to estimate numbers of sand: (1) perimeter of earth ≈ 3,000,000 stadia max; (2) diameter of earth > moon and diameter of sun > earth; (3) diameter of sun ≈ 30× diameter of moon max; (4) diameter of sun > side of chiliagon inscribed in greatest circle of the 'universe' (proved by experiment); (5) a poppy-seed contains ≤ 10,000 grains and diameter ≥ 1/4 finger-breadth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes states these assumptions explicitly to produce conservative upper bounds for the diameter of the universe and for the number of grains of sand. He explains experimental methods (rod+mask) for estimating the solar angle and justifies parameter choices by referencing prior astronomers (Aristarchus, Eudoxus, Pheidias).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number-naming scheme — orders and periods (The Sand-Reckoner)
rubrics_metrics.description: A systematic scheme for naming and representing very large numbers using orders and periods based on 10^8 (a myriad-myriad) as a unit and iterated orders and periods: first period consists of orders up to (10^8)^10^8, second period uses that as unit, and so on up to huge exponents (construction of P and higher periods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes uses this scheme to express numbers far larger than previously named, explaining first/second/... periods and orders and illustrating with 'octads' (geometric progression terms 1,10,10^2,...) and a theorem about products of terms in continued proportion. The scheme is constructive and intended to show some named numbers exceed counts of sand even for universe-sized spheres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem on geometric progression terms (octads)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a series in continued proportion has first term 1 and second 10 (i.e. 1,10,10^2,...), then for any two terms A_m, A_n their product A_m·A_n is also a term of the series, located as many terms from the beginning as the sum (minus one) of the term indices — i.e. the usual index addition property in geometric progressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes states and proves this general property about geometric progressions and uses it to organize 'octads' spanning his orders and periods scheme; this theorem underpins placement of very large named numbers within the naming framework.
